job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Hana Alvarez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My mornings start with breakfast for my grandmother, Nana Pilar, who lives with us, and then I take the bus to the church hall where I help run the Tuesday and Thursday food pantry. The rest of the day is applications, usually at the kitchen table in Verdan. I live with my parents, my father is a bus mechanic, and my mother teaches at the primary school.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What did you study, and what was your internship?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Finance and banking, with a good result. I spent eight weeks at the Verdan Community Credit Union, in member services. I helped people with loan forms and answered questions at the counter. I use AI now and then, mostly to translate or tidy forms for members who find the language hard, but I check it by hand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, though I never expected it to be a miracle either. At church I'd say the important things don't change: people still need someone to explain their finances kindly. I'd tell my fiancé Mateo it means our plans stay as they are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it means the hunt goes on at the same pace and my future depends on whether a community bank has an opening. A little automation will take the form-filling, which I did on my internship, but the counter work is still people. So I'm hopeful, though with no offer yet I'm not at ease.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep applying to credit unions, community banks and the town hall's finance office, about eight a week. I'd keep volunteering at the pantry because I like it and it keeps me in the community. And I'd go on putting money aside for the wedding, which we're planning for two years from now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopeful, but with a stone in my shoe. I'm fine until I think of the months going by.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a community bank in particular?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Why a community bank in particular?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How are the wedding plans affected by your job search?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I saw one woman at the credit union cry with relief when we found her a smaller loan payment. That's the work I want to do, and I couldn't picture it at a big bank where you're a number on a screen.

say: I'd say good, but I never expected a **miracle**: people still need someone to explain finances kindly.
I'd tell my fiancé Mateo our plans stay as they are.

do: Apply to credit unions, community banks and the **town hall** finance office, eight a week.
Keep volunteering at the church food pantry.
Keep saving for the **wedding** in two years.
feel: **Hopeful**, with a stone in my shoe when I think of the months passing.

Put money aside each month for the wedding

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a big change, but people have handled big changes before, and we should help each other do it. At church I'd say we should teach older folks how to use the new systems, so they aren't left out. At the credit union I'd say the personal touch matters even more when the machines take over the forms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the forms and the checking go first. That was a large part of what I did, and the credit union might hire one counter person where it used to hire three. But the member who needs help with a hard conversation still needs a human, and I think I'm good at that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the new loan systems properly and ask the credit union manager, Mrs Reyes, if I could trial them as a volunteer. I'd also apply to the town hall's benefits office. I'd keep helping at the pantry, and I'd offer a class for older members on online banking. And I'd keep my savings steady, only a little for the wedding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy, but not frightened. I feel I can find my place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you really run a class for older members?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Would you really run a class for older members?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Mrs Reyes want to see from a volunteer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. My Nana Pilar can't use her banking app, and she isn't alone. If I stand in the church hall once a month and show twenty people how to check a balance, I'm useful and I'm also practising what I'd do in the job.

say: I'd say people have handled big change before and should help each other, especially **older folks**.
I'd say the personal touch matters more when machines take the forms.

Apply to the town hall **benefits office**.
Offer a class for older members on online banking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to look after each other and the government must step in. At church I'd ask us to prepare a rota of families who can lend a hand if a household loses its income. I'd say that two years is too short for anyone to be ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'm afraid. My whole plan was a counter job at a community bank, and a bank can do with almost no one at the counter if the machines are as good as they say. Mateo is an electrician, so his work would last longer, but I'd feel I was letting my side down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply to anything that puts a person in front of a person, a school office, a clinic, a parish office. I'd put my savings aside and keep the wedding small. I'd ask my mother whether I could train as a teaching assistant. And I'd use my pantry contacts to find out what services will exist when people need them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, and also guilty for feeling scared when so many others have it harder. I pray about it, too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a small wedding mean to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What would a small wedding mean to you?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you really train as a teaching assistant?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It would mean Mateo and me, our families and the church hall. No big band, no hundred guests. Honestly, that's the wedding I always pictured, and I'd feel a bit relieved, even though it came about the wrong way.

say: I'd say we must look after each other and **government must step in**.
I'd ask church to set up a rota of families who help a household that loses income.
think: My whole plan was a counter job, and a bank can manage with **almost no one** at the counter.
Mateo's electrical work would last longer, but I'd feel I'd let my side down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a mercy, and we should use it to prepare, not argue. I'd ask the town to set up a small training fund. At work I'd say train your staff now, because the ones you keep will be the ones who learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel more hopeful. If I get a place at a credit union this year, I'd have four years to become the person who knows the members and the systems both. That's a person they'd keep. But I know there are no guarantees, and that keeps me praying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take any role at a community bank or credit union, even part-time. I'd go for a banking certificate in the evenings. I'd learn the systems fast, since I'm steady but I do get there, and I'd keep the pantry work. I'd marry Mateo in two years as planned, and save a quarter of my pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer than the quick one. Heavy, but I'd be able to breathe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to the manager to get a part-time role?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What would you say to the manager to get a part-time role?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would marrying in two years change your plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, give me three months. Let me do the counter, the forms and the phone, and I'll learn whatever you throw at me. I'd also say my Nana Pilar's whole street banks with you, and I know them. That counts for something.

I'd urge the town to set up a small training fund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time to teach people and build something good. I'd say to my family that we should keep faith and keep saving. I'd tell young people to learn how to talk to people, because that's what lasts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I feel at peace. In ten years Mateo and I could have a home, a child, maybe two, and I could be working as a branch manager or running the member advice side. The thing to watch is that I don't get comfortable and stop learning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd find a job at a community bank in the next year, finish my certificate, and learn the new tools as they come. I'd marry in two years and buy a small house by 28. I'd keep helping at the pantry and the church. And I'd start saving for a child, because I want one before 30.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Peaceful, and grateful. It's the picture where I can still see the life I'd always wanted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would stop you from getting comfortable?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What would stop you from getting comfortable?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would a child change the plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably Nana Pilar. My grandma says a person who stops learning goes stale, and she's 84 and still learning to text. If she can do it, I can keep up too.

I'd tell young people to learn how to talk to people.
think: At peace: a home, a child or two, and maybe a **branch manager** role by then.
The risk is getting comfortable and ceasing to learn.
do: Find a community bank job within a year and finish my **certificate**.
Marry in two years and buy a small house by 28.
feel: **Peaceful** and grateful: I can still see the life I always wanted.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one, since my whole picture was a counter job and two years gives no time to find another way. What would help is employers who still hire beginners, quick training near home, and communities that look after people who lose work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Just that I'm not a quick person with new things. I get there, but I get there slowly, and I'd like people to be patient with someone like me.

headlineQuote: I get there, but I get there slowly, and I'd like people to be patient with someone like me.
portrait: Hana is 23, a finance graduate in Verdan, living with her parents and her grandmother Nana Pilar, with no offer yet.
She volunteers at the church food pantry and wants a counter job at a **community bank**.
Her traditional views favour family, faith, community and learning on the job over handouts.
She is steady with tools, slower than some but reliable, and turns threats into **service**.
She is anxious when the counter job might vanish, and peaceful when she sees time for a **wedding and family**.
biggestWorry: The **AGI by 2028** picture worries her most, because her whole plan was a counter job.
whatWouldHelp: Employers who still hire **beginners** and quick training near home.
Communities that look after people who lose work.
